entry.evidence: There is no consensus about the upper mantle discontinuities and the interpretation of quantitative observations

steps.action: Frame the open question of the depth, nature and origin of upper-mantle discontinuities (MLD, ILD, Lehmann, LAB), and argue that controlled-source nuclear-explosion data resolve mantle phases better than passive methods.
steps.quote: There is no consensus about the upper mantle discontinuities and the interpretation of quantitative observations

steps.action: List published rival mechanisms for the MLD (grain size, composition, water/carbonatite, partial melt, anisotropy) and for the Lehmann discontinuity.
steps.quote: Many mechanisms have been proposed to explain the origin of MLD

steps.action: Use the 3 September 2017 North Korean nuclear test (mb 6.3) as the seismic source, recorded by permanent and portable broadband stations grouped into five corridors.
steps.quote: On 3 September 2017, North Korea conducted its sixth nuclear test near the China-Korea border

steps.action: Correct traveltimes to a constant 30 km crust with RAYINVR and the NCcrust model, filter (0.1–3 Hz) and plot reduced sections, and identify PmP, PmPPmP, P, PxP, PxPPmP, PL and P410, delayed first arrivals near 950 km and a scattered coda.
steps.quote: The observed arrivals (Fig. 2a) can be classified into two categories.

steps.action: Note that the five corridors show similar features and interpret one representative densely sampled profile (profile 1).
steps.quote: All five profiles show very similar features

steps.action: Pick phase onsets (100–150 ms accuracy) and fit traveltimes of refractions and reflections with RAYINVR to obtain a 1-D background velocity model, with 500 ms residuals.
steps.quote: was used to obtain a 1D velocity model by fitting travel times of both refraction and reflection phases

steps.action: Recompute the average crustal velocity without the crustal static correction and find the same value, within 6.05–6.25 km/s.
steps.quote: We have checked the velocity that would result without crustal correction (Fig. S2)

steps.action: Infer from the background model a PxP reflector at ~75 km, a sharp, high-impedance-contrast Moho, an LVZ below 120 km, the Lehmann discontinuity at ~220 km and the 410 at ~410 km.
steps.quote: We interpret the PxP phase as a primary reflection phase from an intra-lithospheric reflector at about 75 km depth.

steps.action: Set up reflectivity-method synthetics with an earth-flattening transformation and define three visual acceptance criteria for synthetic sections.
steps.quote: The synthetic section is regarded acceptable if it matches the following three criteria

steps.action: Compare synthetics for negative and several positive ILD velocity contrasts with the data and select a positive contrast of +0.15 km/s.
steps.quote: The model with a contrast of + 0.15 km/s (Fig. 6b) provides the best match between synthetic and observed waveforms and amplitudes

steps.action: Vary the MLD contrast, the Lehmann gradient and the LVZ average velocity in synthetics, and select an LVZ of ~8.05 km/s with no sharp contrast at the MLD or Lehmann discontinuity.
steps.quote: Model (Fig. 7e) with an average velocity about 8.05 km/s in the LVZ provides the best match between synthetic and observed waveforms and amplitudes

steps.action: Name rival depth origins of the scattered coda: lower-crustal scattering, thin sub-Moho anomalies (Ryberg et al.), multiple crustal scattering (Nielsen and Thybo), and LVZ random fluctuations (Nielsen et al.).
steps.quote: Seismic scattering has been observed from several depth ranges.

steps.action: Compute reflectivity synthetics with Gaussian random velocity layers (L = 2–5 km, σ = 4 %) placed in three depth zones: Moho–ILD, ILD–MLD, and LVZ.
steps.quote: we test three different scattering zones

steps.action: Compare each synthetic with the observed section: the background model and the shallower zones fail, while LVZ scattering resembles the data.
steps.quote: The synthetic section (Fig. 8d) for fluctuations in the low-velocity zone leads to scattering similar to observation (Fig. 8a).

steps.action: Reject scatterers above the ILD (insufficient coda) and between the ILD and MLD (scattered phases arriving before Pn).
steps.quote: Models with scatterers solely above the ILD cannot explain our observations as they do not create sufficient coda to the P (Fig. 8b).

steps.action: Keep strong heterogeneity in the upper-mantle LVZ as the preferred model.
steps.quote: [...] model for the mantle beneath the northeastern SKC includes strong heterogeneity in the upper-mantle low-velocity zone.

steps.action: Scan layer thickness L (1–10 km) and fluctuation σ (2–6 %) at Q = 500, and estimate L of 2–7 km and σ of about 4 %.
steps.quote: [...] parameter space of L and σ in the ranges of 1–10 km and 2–6 % (1 % steps)

steps.action: Vary LVZ attenuation Q for the preferred L and σ, and estimate Q between 500 and 800.
steps.quote: Models with Q values between 500 and 800 in the LVZ fit the observations well

steps.action: Present the final 1-D fine-scale model (thin, low-velocity crust; strong Moho; ILD; heterogeneous LVZ) with synthetic sections.
steps.quote: We present a 1D fine-scale crust and uppermost lithospheric mantle structure

steps.action: Compare the ILD depth with independent autocorrelogram and S-receiver-function results in the NE SKC and report consistency.
steps.quote: which is consistent with results obtained by the auto correlogram method

steps.action: Set out the thermal, compositional and anisotropic rival mechanisms for the ILD and MLD (Table 2, Fig. 13).
steps.quote: Until now, various mechanisms (Table 2) have been proposed to explain the origin of the MLD (and the ILD)

steps.action: Compute regional geotherms from surface heat flow (60 ± 10 mW/m2) and set them against peridotite solidi with water and CO2.
steps.quote: We calculate the regional geotherms based on surface heat flow data

steps.action: Find that the temperature at the MLD is below or close to the carbonated-peridotite solidus.
steps.quote: the corresponding temperature at the (upper) MLD is below or close to the solidus of carbonated peridotite

steps.action: Keep partial melting (near-solidus rocks) as the likely cause of the MLD and LVZ.
steps.quote: [...] the MLD is likely caused by the presence of partial melting.

steps.action: Reject grain-boundary sliding, olivine grain-size variation, Mg# decrease and (in Table 2) hydrous minerals as causes of the observed ILD/MLD, arguing from the sign of the velocity change and the required conditions.
steps.quote: Therefore, the origin of the ILD cannot be a decrease from high-Mg# (Fo>=92) to low-Mg# (Fo <91).

steps.action: Keep the spinel-to-garnet transition as the ILD origin, matching its depth (~85 km) and its positive velocity change.
steps.quote: this phase transformation represents a velocity increase, which is consistent with our ILD observation.

steps.action: Pose two rival explanations of the extremely thin seismic lower crust and the strong Moho: eclogitization of the lower crust, or strong horizontal anisotropy.
steps.quote: This observation may have two explanations

steps.action: Down-weight eclogitization because eclogite-facies rocks are not found at the surface, retaining it only as unlikely.
steps.quote: we mention it as a possible, but unlikely, alternative explanation

steps.action: Build a tectonic history (Pacific subduction weakening, slab retreat, drip delamination, horizontal lower-crustal flow) that produces frozen-in anisotropy in a thin lower crust.
steps.quote: anisotropic thin lower crust can be roughly inferred by the following process

steps.action: Keep anisotropy as required at the Moho, because the 1.8 km/s isotropic contrast cannot reproduce the PmP and PmPPmP amplitudes.
steps.quote: The reflector strength requires anisotropy as even the observed 1.8 km/s contrast cannot reproduce the observed PmP and PmPPmp amplitudes.

end.claim: Beneath the NE Sino-Korean Craton, the nuclear-explosion sections are fitted by a 1-D model with: a 30 km, low-velocity (~6.17 km/s) crust above an exceptionally strong Moho; a positive ILD at ~75 km; and a heterogeneous LVZ (~8.05 km/s; L 2–7 km, σ 4 %, Q 500–800) between the MLD at ~120 km and the Lehmann discontinuity.

decisive_move.sentence: Reflectivity synthetics for trial 1-D models, judged visually against the observed sections, fix the ILD contrast, the LVZ velocity and the scattering parameters; without them the model would rest on traveltimes alone.

gates.evidence: The data are opportunistic recordings of a nuclear test by permanent networks; no hypothesis directed acquisition (p. 2). The trial synthetics could fail, and several did (Figs. 6–10, p. 3–5). However, fits are visual, and the mechanism verdicts (spinel–garnet, partial melt, anisotropy from drip flow) rest on qualitative literature arguments. The acceptance criteria (p. 3) are stated, but nothing shows they were fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: An underground nuclear test (North Korea, 3 Sept 2017; USGS event parameters) used as a controlled seismic source

novelty_claims.quote: It is an exceptional result that the average crustal velocity is 6.2 km/s for a crustal thickness [...] .
[...] our unique observations of a very thin crust for a cratonic region and exceptionally strong Moho reflections.
explains our unique seismic observations of a thin crust with low average velocity and low vertical velocity gradient

limits:
The XML text supplied holds only the abstract and captions, so body steps cite printed pages. The paper reports internal inconsistencies:
- ILD contrast: 'from 8.05 to ~8.10 km/s' (p. 3) versus +0.15 km/s and 8.05 to ~8.20 km/s (p. 3, p. 6, Fig. 6b).
- ILD depth: 75 km versus 'similar depth (85 km)' (p. 6).
- Crustal thickness: 'ca 0.30 km' (p. 5, a typo).
- Average crustal velocity: 6.15, 6.17 and 6.2 km/s.
- Station count: 291+7 (p. 2) versus 80 permanent + 7 temporary (p. 5).
- LVZ depth: 120–190 km (abstract) versus 120–220 km (p. 4).
- Coda duration: 4 s (abstract), ~5 s (p. 2), 8–13 s (p. 4).
- Hydrous minerals: 'may explain our observation of the ILD' (p. 10), but rejected (-) in Table 2.
- Lower crust: 'thinning of the lower crust to the present thickness of only 30 km' (p. 13) versus seismic lower crust < 3 km (p. 12).

Fits are judged visually; no quantitative misfit, formal uncertainty or resolution test is given beyond pick accuracy, residuals and ray coverage (Fig. 5b). Only profile 1 is modelled, and the claim that all five profiles are similar is asserted, not quantified. The claim that the Moho reflector 'requires anisotropy' (p. 13) is not supported by shown anisotropic modelling (inference). No review file was supplied.

Sub-claim statuses:
- ILD from the spinel–garnet transition: best_explanation.
- MLD/LVZ from partial melt or near-solidus rocks: best_explanation.
- Moho anisotropy from drip-related lower-crustal flow: best_explanation at most; the authors 'speculate' (abstract).
- LVZ heterogeneity parameters (L, σ, Q): estimate_with_resolution.
- Eclogitization: retained as an unlikely alternative.

disagreements.support: Traveltimes and synthetics need a much lower LVZ velocity and a smaller vertical gradient than IASP91 beneath the NE SKC.
disagreements.quote: The average velocity of this LVZ is about 8.05 km/s, which is much lower than the IASP91 standard model.

disagreements.target: Global average continental crust (Christensen and Mooney, 1995)
disagreements.support: Ray-tracing gives an average crustal velocity of ~6.17 km/s for a 30 km crust, far below the global average.
disagreements.quote: This average crustal velocity is extraordinarily lower than the global average for the continental crust

disagreements.target: Ryberg et al. (2000) sub-Moho thin-anomaly scattering model
disagreements.support: The paper cites Nielsen and Thybo (2003) against it; its own synthetics with shallow scatterers fail to produce the observed coda.
disagreements.quote: However, Nielsen and Thybo (2003) demonstrate that this mechanism does not match the observed amplitude characteristics

disagreements.target: Elastically accommodated grain-boundary sliding (Karato et al., 2015)
disagreements.support: The temperature is compatible, but the mechanism may not produce enough velocity change; it is rejected in Table 2.
disagreements.quote: it is debated if this mechanism can generate sufficient velocity variation to explain our observed MLD or ILD

disagreements.target: Olivine grain-size explanation of the LVZ (Faul and Jackson, 2005)
disagreements.support: The mechanism is argued to require wet mantle, so it cannot explain a cratonic LVZ without water or melt.
disagreements.quote: The mechanism cannot explain the presence of the seismic LVZ in cratonic mantle in the absence of water or melt.

disagreements.target: Mg# decrease as cause of the discontinuity (Schutt and Lesher, 2006; Tang et al., 2008)
disagreements.support: There is no evidence of an abrupt Mg# change, and a decrease would lower velocity, whereas the observed ILD is a velocity increase.
disagreements.quote: Therefore, the origin of the ILD cannot be a decrease from high-Mg# (Fo>=92) to low-Mg# (Fo <91).
